title: From Betrayal to Forgiveness
lead: The evil others plan against us, God can turn to good. A family’s past does not have to decide its future.
questions: In which of your relationships does remorse need to stop being a feeling and become different behavior the next time a similar situation comes up?
What old pit lies hidden in your family, one everyone knows about and no one mentions, and what is the smallest step you could take toward it?
Whom have you forgiven in a way that still leaves them carrying shame around you, and how can that forgiveness be finished?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Joseph’s story is the longest narrative in Genesis and also the quietest: it contains not a single visible miracle. God works through an arrangement of small things, through dreams, through one person’s memory and another person’s forgetting. It begins with a special robe, with which a father singled Joseph out in front of his older brothers, and with a hatred that grew quietly even before Jacob’s favorite put it on for the first time. Then comes the pit at Dothan: the brothers threw the seventeen-year-old into it and then “sat down to eat a meal.” That he cried out for mercy we learn only years later, from their own lips. A wrong we have brushed aside does not disappear. It waits inside us for its time.

In the account of Joseph’s years in Egypt, we are told four times that the LORD was with him, and two of those times he is in prison. God’s presence did not keep him out of the dungeon; it was protection in the middle of misery, not protection from hardship. When famine forced the brothers to travel to Egypt, Joseph recognized them and decided to test them. He recreated the situation from years before, singled out Benjamin in front of everyone, and watched. No one took offense. And when a planted cup gave them the chance to leave Rachel’s son in slavery, Judah, the same Judah who once counted the silver, pleaded: “Please let your servant stay here… in place of the boy.” Remorse is not a feeling. Remorse is different behavior in a similar situation. That is when Joseph revealed himself: “I am Joseph, your brother… the one you sold into Egypt!” And he added the sentence that is the heart of this story: “it was not you who sent me here, but God.”

After their father’s death, the brothers’ fear came back; they sent a plea for forgiveness, hiding behind the dead man. Joseph wept, because after all these years they still thought they needed a go-between to come to him. He answered, “What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.” He did not deny their guilt; he handed judgment over it to the Most High. And then he promised to provide for their children and “spoke kindly to them.” He tried to lift from them not only the fear of punishment but also the weight of shame. Reconciliation doesn’t end with giving up on punishment. The measure of this family’s healing was not Joseph’s career but the fact that at last they could weep together.

Yesterday we read how God transformed Jacob at the Jabbok. Today we look at his sons and see that a father’s experience does not pass to his children along with the family name. Joseph’s story is the longest narrative in Genesis and also the quietest. There are no burning bushes, no open heavens, no wrestling in the night. God speaks only once in it, and not to Joseph, but to old Jacob before his journey to Egypt. Everything else happens through dreams, coincidences, one person’s memory and another person’s forgetting. Here God works through an arrangement of small things. That is good news for people whose lives are also made up mostly of small things.

sections.heading: A Robe Woven in Front of Everyone
paragraphs: “Now Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons, because Joseph had been born to him in his old age; so he made him a robe of many colors,” or, as other translations have it, a long robe with sleeves. This was no cheap trinket from the market. The Bible uses the same term to describe what a king’s daughters wore. It was the garment of someone who does not work with his hands. A robe like that was woven at home over weeks, so the whole family watched it take shape and knew who it was for. The hatred of the ten brothers grew while the cloth was on the loom, long before Joseph ever put on his father’s gift. The text says, “they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him.” On top of the favoritism came the dreams of sheaves and stars bowing down to Joseph. This story begins with something we know from our own homes and churches: a preference that lifts some people up in front of others. Being chosen, worn like a long robe for show, doesn’t awaken faith in the One who chooses. It awakens hatred for the one chosen.

sections.heading: The Pit and the Meal
paragraphs: At Dothan the brothers saw him coming from far off. “Here comes that dreamer!… Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him. Then we shall see what becomes of his dreams!” They stripped him of his robe and threw him into a dry pit. Then comes a sentence that no commentary can soften: “they sat down to eat a meal.” A few steps from their meal, in a waterless hole, sat a seventeen-year-old. Did he cry out? The whole chapter doesn’t say a word about it. We find out only years later, from the brothers themselves: “We are certainly guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn’t listen” (WEB). The narrator kept silent about that cry and let the brothers who ignored it be the ones to tell us. A wrong we brush aside does not disappear. It waits inside a person for its hour. When a caravan came along carrying balm and spices, Judah floated an idea: why kill him? Let’s sell him. They got twenty shekels of silver for him, exactly what later law would set as the value of a boy his age. Brothers sold their brother like a slave.

sections.heading: The LORD Was with Joseph
paragraphs: In the chapter about Potiphar’s house and the prison, we are told four times that the LORD was with Joseph. Twice when Joseph is promoted, and twice when, after a false accusation, he is sitting in a dungeon. God’s presence did not keep him out of the dungeon. It was protection in the middle of misery, not rescue from it. And it was concrete. In prison God didn’t give Joseph a warm feeling and the scent of roses; He extended kindness to him, “granting him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.” He changed events, not just moods. And the road from the dungeon to the palace began with a small thing. One morning Joseph noticed that two fellow prisoners looked downcast and asked them why. He didn’t start with a lecture about God; he waited until they said it themselves: “We both had dreams… but there is no one to interpret them.” The best witness answers a need that has already been spoken. Sadly, the chapter ends with one of the saddest sentences in the book: “The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.” The good we fail to do often comes from neglecting good decisions or, in the kinder version, from a fleeting memory. We promise to get in touch, to check on it, to come back to the matter… The cupbearer remembered two years later.

sections.heading: Forgetting and Fruitfulness
paragraphs: Pharaoh’s dream lifted Joseph out of the dungeon to the second place in the kingdom. Egypt’s new governor married and gave his sons names like two boundary stones. Manasseh: “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.” Ephraim: “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” His firstborn’s name speaks of forgetting his father’s house, and yet he had not forgotten his family: when his brothers stand before him, he will recognize them in an instant. What he forgot was the pain. And that very healing made possible everything that came after. A person who is still bleeding cannot lead anyone through reconciliation.

sections.heading: Same Situation, Different People
paragraphs: Years later, famine drove the brothers to Egypt for grain. Joseph recognized them; they did not recognize him. And something began that looks from the outside like a cruel game but is actually a test. Joseph partly recreates the experience of losing one’s freedom, which he knew firsthand, and watches how the brothers will treat Benjamin. He heard them talking among themselves, not knowing he understood: “We are certainly guilty concerning our brother” (WEB). He turned aside and wept. But words aren’t enough; remorse has to be tested. At the feast he seated them in front of him and had Benjamin served a portion “five times larger than any of the others.” He recreated exactly the arrangement that had once driven them to their crime: Rachel’s youngest son singled out in front of everyone. And he watched. No one took offense. Then came the cup planted in Benjamin’s sack. They could have left Rachel’s son in slavery and gone home free. Back then they were guilty and indifferent. Now they are innocent, and they go back. They tear their clothes and return to the city. Remorse is not a feeling. Remorse is different behavior in a similar situation.

sections.heading: In Place of the Boy
paragraphs: That is when Judah steps forward. The same Judah who counted the silver at the pit. His speech in Benjamin’s defense is the longest plea in all of Genesis that one person makes to another, and the word “father” comes back in it more than a dozen times. The man who once sold Jacob’s favorite now brings up his father’s love for another favorite without a trace of envy, as the very reason for his request: “Now please let your servant stay here as my lord’s slave in place of the boy.” In place of. The same words describe the ram offered in place of Isaac on Moriah. The one who sold his brother for silver now offers himself as the substitute. And that is when Joseph breaks. Not at the sight of his brothers or of Benjamin. At the words: take me instead of him. His brothers have passed the test.

sections.heading: I Am Joseph
paragraphs: “I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?” The brothers “were unable to answer him, because they were terrified in his presence.” He had to say it a second time and add the one proof no stranger could have known: “I am Joseph, your brother… the one you sold into Egypt!” To prove who he was, he had to name out loud what they had done to him. Reconciliation doesn’t go around the truth; it goes through it. And right after that he speaks the sentence that is the heart of the whole story: “it was not you who sent me here, but God.” Joseph doesn’t claim the Lord wanted their evil act. He says God intercepted it and turned it into rescue for many. He sent them back to their father with wagons and gifts, and as they left, he called after them: “Do not quarrel on the way!” The Hebrew word used here carries both quarreling and fear, which is why some translations render it as a call not to be afraid on the way. They probably needed both. People who have just been forgiven can spend the whole trip home tallying up who was more to blame.

sections.heading: Am I in the Place of God?
paragraphs: Seventeen years later Jacob dies. And it turns out that the brothers’ fear has survived all those years under Joseph’s roof: “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him.” They send him word that before he died their father told them to ask for forgiveness. The narrator records no such instruction anywhere; perhaps it is the last trick of a family in which deception was the mother tongue. They say, “please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.” Your father, not ours. Even in asking for mercy, they cannot stand beside their brother, only beneath him, and they hide behind the dead. “When their message came to him, Joseph wept.” He weeps because nearly forty years after that pit, they are still afraid of him. Because they think they need a go-between and a written petition to approach their own brother. It’s the first time any of them has asked him outright for forgiveness, and he had forgiven them long ago. Guilt that was never confessed tormented them longer than the wrong their brother suffered.

Joseph’s answer begins with a question: “Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?” That sentence had been spoken in this family once before. Jacob once hurled it at childless Rachel, in anger and helplessness. The same words can push a person away or lift their fear. It depends on who says them and in what spirit. And then comes the sentence this story is in the Bible for: “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this, to preserve the lives of many people.” Joseph doesn’t say nothing happened. He says it plainly: you intended evil. Forgiveness doesn’t deny guilt; it hands judgment over it to God. And he takes one more step: “I will provide for you and your little ones.” So Joseph reassured his brothers and “spoke kindly to them.” He not only lifted their fear of punishment; he also wanted to free them from the weight of shame. Reconciliation doesn’t end with giving up on punishment.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Today we close the section “There Is Hope When the Promise Is Far Away.” In Joseph’s life the promise was far away for decades, and God did not perform a single visible miracle in this story. He worked underneath: through the order in which two prisoners told their dreams, through the cupbearer’s memory and forgetting, through the arrangement of portions on a table. Only looking back can you see what He was doing all along. Most of our stories look just like that. And in many families, including families of believers, there is a pit like that from years ago: a wrong everyone knows about but no one mentions. This reading does not promise that reconciliation will come quickly. Here it took decades to ripen and needed time on both sides: the brothers had to grow into asking, and Joseph had to assure them yet again that he was not seeking revenge. The measure of this family’s healing was not Joseph’s career or a rescued Egypt, but the fact that at last they could weep together.
